pages.name: The Three Cycles
pages.html:
A wizard's strength moves with their god's moon. This is arithmetic, not metaphor, and it is why the Conclave schedules everything the way it does.

Three moons, three cycles, none of them matching:

MoonGodOrderCycle
Solinari (silver)SolinariWhite Robes36 days
Lunitari (red)LunitariRed Robes28 days
Nuitari (black)NuitariBlack Robes8 days

Nuitari's short cycle means Black Robes swing between strength and weakness roughly once a week, which is a fair summary of the Order generally. Solinari's long cycle means White Robes have predictable, well-telegraphed peaks, which is also a fair summary.

Nuitari is invisible. Only those who serve him can see the black moon at all — to everyone else it is a hole where stars should be, if they know to look, which almost nobody does. A character who can casually report the black moon's phase has told you something about themselves.

Tracking It

The module includes a calendar widget that does this for you. It sits on screen showing the Krynn date and all three moons at their true phases, and the GM advances it a day at a time or jumps by week or month. High sanction is ringed in gold, low sanction in crimson.

Nuitari is hidden from players by default, because the black moon is invisible to all but those who serve it. There is a setting to reveal it, and a character who can casually report the black moon's phase has told you something about themselves.

If you would rather not track a calendar at all, roll a d6 at dawn for each Order that matters at your table:

d6Phase
1Low sanction — the moon is dark
2–5Waxing or waning — no effect
6High sanction — the moon is full

Roll it in the open. It takes four seconds and it makes every wizard at the table look up.

pages.name: Reading the Three Moons
pages.html:
The moons are not a traffic-light system for power. They create a changing political climate that every trained wizard reads differently.

Solinari

The long silver cycle rewards planning. White Robes schedule wards, examinations, and difficult acts of protection near the full moon, then use the waning weeks for patient work. At low sanction they become conservative with magic, relying on allies and prepared sanctuaries. A White Robe forced into haste under a dark Solinari is outside the life they designed.

Lunitari

The red moon completes its cycle with the calendar month, making Red Robe institutions unnervingly punctual. High sanction favors invention, negotiation, transformation, and public demonstrations. During low sanction, Red Robes trade information, revise theories, and allow rivals to underestimate them. They are the Order most likely to treat weakness as a scheduled resource.

Nuitari

The black moon turns quickly and is seen only by those attuned to it. Black Robes live with frequent reversals. Their plans use short windows, layered contingencies, and proxies who need not understand why a date matters. High sanction makes decisive action tempting; low sanction arrives soon enough to punish anyone who mistakes momentum for permanence.

At the Table

  • Announce a moon's visible phase when a wizard of its Order enters an important scene.
  • Let NPC plans reveal lunar literacy: an ambush postponed by two nights is information.
  • Give players access to the same calendar their enemies use. The satisfaction comes from planning better, not from discovering a hidden modifier after the roll.
  • Use low sanction to change methods, not to make a wizard irrelevant. A weakened archmage still has apprentices, bargains, scrolls, and a locked door.

pages.name: Sanction Mechanics
pages.html:
These apply only to a Wizard of High Sorcery — a character who has passed the Test and taken a robe. Renegades, sorcerers, warlocks, bards, and unaffiliated casters are unaffected. The gift is conditional on the oath.

High Sanction

While your moon is full, you gain the following:

  • Once per turn, add your proficiency bonus to the damage of one spell you cast.
  • You may cast one spell per long rest as though using a slot one level higher, without expending the higher slot.
  • Advantage on Arcana checks and on saving throws against being counterspelled or dispelled.

Low Sanction

While your moon is dark:

  • Your spell save DC and spell attack bonus are reduced by 2.
  • You cannot cast your highest-level available spell slot. It is simply not there when you reach for it.
  • Disadvantage on Constitution saves made to maintain concentration.

Two Moons at Once

Effects do not stack across Orders — a wizard has one moon. But when a rival Order is in high sanction and yours is in low, the difference is felt. This is the single most important scheduling fact in Krynnish politics, and any NPC wizard planning a confrontation has checked.

DM Note — Weaponising the Calendar

Let the players discover this rather than explaining it. The moment a party works out that they should attack the Black Robe on a specific night, and then works out that he knows that too, the mechanic has paid for itself.

Raistlin, notably, does not appear to suffer low sanction. He has never explained this and the Conclave has stopped asking. (Whichever agenda you selected, the answer is the same: he is not drawing solely on Nuitari, and something else is making up the difference.)

pages.name: Conjunctions, Omens, and Campaign Clocks
pages.html:
One full moon is power. Two are politics. Three are history.

Two Moons in Strength

When two Orders stand in high sanction, their rivalry becomes visible. The Conclave schedules contested votes then only when it wants both sides confident enough to bargain. Joint rituals gain stability if the casters agree on purpose and become volatile if they agree only on wording. No extra numerical bonus is required; use the conjunction to justify larger magic and sharper demands.

One High, One Low

This is the calendar of coups, arrests, challenges, and surprise diplomacy. An Order in strength will insist that timing is coincidence. An Order in weakness will have prepared for the insult. Before an important wizard conflict, ask which side chose the date. The answer tells you who believes they are in control.

The Night of the Eye

All three full moons do not make every spell automatically succeed. They remove ceilings. A working may reach farther, bind more participants, or alter something normally too deeply rooted to move. The cost and the required decision remain. In fact, power on this scale should make consent and purpose more important, because there is no technical failure left to blame.

Campaign Clock

Time remainingSignalEscalation
Six sessionsAn astrologer names the alignment and refuses to explain why they are afraid.Factions begin acquiring components and securing promises.
Four sessionsTwo unrelated enemies choose the same deadline.The Conclave restricts travel through Wayreth.
Two sessionsRitual sites are occupied; missing relics surface.Every faction offers the party a version of the truth.
One sessionThe moons are visible together before dawn.Plans can no longer remain secret without becoming irrelevant.
TonightThe widget marks all three full.Ask what each major NPC attempts while impossibility is briefly negotiable.

pages.name: The Night of the Eye
pages.html:
Once every five hundred and four days, all three moons come full together and stand in the sky as a single silver ring around a red iris around a hole of absolute black.

Everyone on Krynn sees it. Nobody enjoys it.

Mechanics

On the Night of the Eye, every Wizard of High Sorcery is in high sanction simultaneously, regardless of Order, and gains the following in addition to the standard benefits:

  • Spells cast are treated as though the caster had a feature allowing them to ignore one condition of their choosing on the spell: material components, somatic components, or verbal components.
  • Any wizard may attempt to cast a spell from another Order's list at DC 15 + spell level (Arcana). This is the only night it is possible, and it is heavily documented in Conclave records as a thing that goes wrong.
  • Rituals of a scale otherwise impossible succeed. Conclave sanction is required. Conclave sanction is rarely granted.

Using It

Put one Night of the Eye in your campaign, place it deliberately, and tell the players roughly when it falls about six sessions in advance. It becomes a clock, and everyone — the party, the Conclave, the Dragonarmies, and the Master — starts planning around the same date.

DM Note — Where to Put It

Directly on your campaign's climax, and let the players find out that the enemy chose that date for the same reason they did.

If you are running the adventure in The Errand of the Black Master, the Night of the Eye falls eleven days after the Conclave convenes, which is the deadline the whole arc runs on.

pages.name: The Calendar Widget
pages.html:
The module tracks the Krynn calendar on screen so you are not doing lunar arithmetic mid-session.

The Calendar

A year on Krynn is 336 days — twelve months of twenty-eight days, four seven-day weeks to the month. Month names are configurable between Solamnic (Newkolt, Deepkolt, Brookgreen…), Ergothi (Aelmont, Rannmont, Mishamont…), and Elven (Winter Night, Winter Deep, Spring Dawning…). It defaults to Solamnic and to the year 350 AC, where Shadow of the Dragon Queen opens.

Using It

  • Arrows step a day at a time. GM only; players see the result immediately.
  • The cog opens the controls — set an exact date, jump by week or month, or jump straight to the next Night of the Eye.
  • Drag it anywhere. Position is saved per user, so your screen layout is yours.
  • Hover a moon for its phase, its Order, and whether it is in sanction.

A moon in high sanction is ringed in gold. A moon in low sanction is ringed in crimson. When all three come full the whole widget lights and a banner appears, and a chat message goes out if you have left that setting on.

Settings

SettingWhat it does
Starting YearThe year the calendar begins at. Default 350 AC.
Calendar NamesSolamnic, Ergothi, or Elven month names.
Moon OffsetsShifts each moon's phase in days. Use these to line the moons up with wherever your campaign already is.
Show Calendar to PlayersOff makes it GM-only. The GM always sees it.
Show Nuitari to PlayersOff by default. The black moon is invisible to all but those who serve it.
Announce the Night of the EyePosts to chat when the moons align.
Show the Calendar WidgetPer-user. Hides the widget for yourself without disabling the module.

For Other Modules and Macros

The calendar exposes an API at game.modules.get("wayreth-black-master").api, also aliased to WayrethCalendar:

CallReturns
getDate()Year, month, day, month name, weekday
getMoons()All three moons with phase and sanction
sanctionFor("black")"high", "low", or null
isNightOfTheEye()Boolean
daysToNightOfTheEye()Days until the next alignment
advance(days)Moves the date. GM only.
setDate(year, month, day)Sets an exact date. GM only.

The hook wayrethCalendarChanged fires on every date change with the full state, so you can drive automation off it.

DM Note — The 504-Day Question

The published sources disagree with themselves. Some give the Night of the Eye as occurring every 420 days, but the three cycles are 36, 28, and 8 days, and those only come full together every 504 days — which is what the 3.5 Campaign Setting states and what the widget computes.

If your campaign needs the alignment on a particular date regardless, use the moon offsets to move it rather than fighting the arithmetic.

pages.name: Other Worlds: Toril and Oerth
pages.html:
The calendar widget is not Krynn-only. Calendar System in module settings switches the whole engine — months, week, year suffix and moons.

SystemYearWeekMoons
Krynn (Solamnic, Ergothi or Elven names)336 days — twelve 28-day months7 daysSolinari 36 · Lunitari 28 · Nuitari 8
Toril — Calendar of Harptos365 days — twelve 30-day months and five festival days10-day tendaySelûne, 30 days
Oerth — Greyhawk Common Year364 days — twelve 28-day months and four 7-day festivals7 daysLuna 28 · Celene 91

What Changes With the System

  • Festival days are real days. Harptos's Midwinter and Greyhawk's Needfest appear in the month picker and the widget marks them.
  • Year suffix follows the world — AC on Krynn, DR on Toril, CY on Oerth.
  • Sanction is Krynn-only. On Toril and Oerth the rings still mark full and new moons, but they are labelled Full and New rather than High and Low Sanction, and the mechanics in this journal do not apply.
  • Moon offsets in settings only affect the Krynn moons. Selûne, Luna and Celene are pre-set to their canonical positions.

Alignments

Krynn: the Night of the Eye, every 504 days.

Oerth: Luna and Celene come full together on Richfest 4 — once every 364 days, so once a year, every year. Celene is also full on the fourth day of each of the four festival weeks, and Luna is full on Fireseek 11.

Toril: none. A single moon has nothing to align with, so the alignment banner and chat announcement are disabled.

DM Note

Switching systems does not convert the current date — it reinterprets the same absolute day count against a different year length, so the displayed date will jump. Set the date again after switching.

The scene darkness sync, the clock and the moonlight setting all work identically on every calendar.
